note: Scripts fed to the Chatterbox/CosyVoice ComfyUI workflow to synthesise the narration now sitting in public/audio/. One sentence per line, each line prefixed [Alice] - that is what the workflow expects to get natural phrasing, and it leans on the punctuation, so keep these grammatical if you re-record. Ids match the step ids in src/lib/tutorial.ts and src/lib/propertyTutorial.ts, and the mp3 for a step is public/audio/<tour>/<id>.mp3 - matching filenames is the entire wiring. Most of these are still PLACEHOLDERS: same voice as the eleven original clips, good enough to hear the whole tour end to end and judge pacing, not final takes. Two are not placeholders any more and were written to be kept: 'welcome' and 'header-clear-cache-test', both re-recorded after the customer flagged them. Whenever a script here changes, the matching step's `body` in tutorial.ts has to change with it word for word - the body is what a screen reader announces, so the two drifting apart means a blind customer and a hearing one are told different things.

tutorial.text:
[Alice] Welcome to WS Inventory Management.
[Alice] I'm your guide, and I'll walk you through the whole app from right here.
[Alice] Nothing is locked, so the page stays live and you can tap anything you like.
[Alice] When I mention a control, it lights up with a soft amber glow.
[Alice] Everything else is in that little bar in the corner: arrows to move, a speaker to mute me, and an X to leave.
[Alice] Tap the forward arrow when you're ready.

[Alice] Light or dark, any time.
[Alice] This flips the whole app between light and dark mode whenever you like.
[Alice] It sticks until you tap it again.

[Alice] This one is the refresh button, and it's safe to try right now.
[Alice] If the app ever looks stuck or out of date, holding this icon gives it a completely fresh start.
[Alice] Go ahead and press and hold it for a moment.
[Alice] While the tour is open it only runs a preview, so nothing on your device will actually be cleared.
[Alice] Outside the tour, holding it clears this device's saved settings and reloads the page.
[Alice] Your inventory itself is never touched.

[Alice] Find anything fast.
[Alice] Search by name, barcode, or location.
[Alice] Next to it, the sort menu can bump low-stock items straight to the top of the list.

[Alice] Bring in, or back up, a whole spreadsheet.
[Alice] Already track inventory in a spreadsheet?
[Alice] Import it here in one go.
[Alice] Export works the same way in reverse, any time you want a copy on hand.

[Alice] Sharing is caring.
[Alice] Send your saved barcode-to-item matches to a teammate, or pull in theirs.
[Alice] It's handy the first time you're both starting from scratch, so neither of you has to scan everything twice.

[Alice] A closer look at these icons.
[Alice] Over on the right, the icons cover breaking down a case, moving stock to another location, editing details, and deleting.
[Alice] Give each one a try, one at a time.

[Alice] Break down a case.
[Alice] Tap this icon to split a sealed case into individual units.
[Alice] It's handy the moment a case actually gets opened, so the count stays accurate at both levels.

[Alice] Move stock somewhere else.
[Alice] Use this one when stock physically moves from one place to another, like a case coming out of the back room and into the front fridge.
[Alice] You say how many units and where they are headed, and the app takes them off this row and puts them on a row for that location.
[Alice] If that location does not have a row for this product yet, one is created for you with the same unit, price, and reorder point.
[Alice] Your total on hand does not change, only where the app thinks it is sitting.

[Alice] Edit the full details.
[Alice] The pencil opens this item's full details, including name, barcode, reorder point, usage tracking window, and more.

[Alice] Delete for good.
[Alice] And the trash icon removes an item entirely.
[Alice] It'll always ask you to confirm first, so there's no risk of an accidental tap losing anything.

[Alice] Two ways to log stock.
[Alice] Barcode mode is for one item at a time.
[Alice] Receipt mode reads a whole photographed receipt at once, which is great right after a big supply run.
[Alice] Accuracy can be hit or miss on a crumpled or blurry receipt, so it's worth a quick double-check of the results before trusting them completely.

[Alice] Scan barcodes or receipts.
[Alice] Tap Scan Barcode and point the camera at any barcode you have to hand.
[Alice] The tour waits quietly while the camera is open, so take as long as you need.
[Alice] Nothing to scan right now?
[Alice] Cancel the camera and we will carry on.

[Alice] What the scan filled in.
[Alice] The barcode lands here, and the description and price fill themselves in whenever the product is one we can look up.
[Alice] Anything left blank is yours to type.
[Alice] Set the quantity, then use Add Stock or Remove to log the movement.

[Alice] Where the filled-in details come from.
[Alice] The small line of text under the barcode tells you what the app found.
[Alice] It checks a shared database built up by other people using this app, and an online product lookup, and fills in whatever either one knows.
[Alice] If it offers a few possible matches instead, pick the closest one, or ignore them and type your own.
[Alice] If it finds nothing, type the name and unit in yourself, and that name joins the shared database when you add the stock, so the next person who scans it does not have to.

[Alice] Treat a looked-up price as a guess.
[Alice] Any price the lookup filled in came from an online listing rather than from your own shelf, so treat it as a rough figure.
[Alice] The app says as much underneath the field while that number is still untouched, and the note disappears the moment you change it.
[Alice] It is worth putting your real cost in, because that is the number your totals are working from.

[Alice] Decide what it searches for.
[Alice] Before you go looking for anything, this row decides what gets typed into the store's search box for you.
[Alice] Auto uses the barcode when the item has one and falls back to the name when it does not.
[Alice] Barcode and Description pin it to one or the other.
[Alice] It is remembered on this device, so it is a one time choice rather than something to think about on every order.

[Alice] Search a store by barcode.
[Alice] Tap Barcode, then tap Find at and pick a store.
[Alice] A barcode is the most exact thing you can hand a retailer, so this usually lands you on the product page itself rather than a page of near misses.
[Alice] It opens in a new tab, so this list stays right where it is.
[Alice] Go and have a look, then come back and tap the arrow.

[Alice] Now search the same store by description.
[Alice] Now tap Description and try the same store again.
[Alice] This is the one you will lean on for anything without a barcode, and for the supplies where any brand will do.
[Alice] The results are broader, so check the size and the pack count before you buy.
[Alice] Whichever of the two you leave selected is the one it will use next time.

[Alice] Jot down a tracking number.
[Alice] Once you've ordered, save the tracking number here for a quick link to the carrier's tracking page.
[Alice] It's simple by design, just a place to keep the number handy, not a live delivery tracker.

[Alice] Send the whole list to a supplier.
[Alice] Tap Share to text or email this entire reorder list straight to a supplier.
[Alice] That's everything currently at or below its reorder point, in one go.

[Alice] Zoom in or out on any time frame.
[Alice] These buttons switch the chart between a week, a month, a few months, or all-time.
[Alice] It's the fastest way to tell a one-off spike apart from a real ongoing trend.

[Alice] Seven days answers what changed.
[Alice] Tap 7d.
[Alice] A week is short enough that one busy day still shows up as a bump, which is what you want when somebody says we are going through these faster than usual.
[Alice] If this number looks nothing like the longer ranges, something changed recently and it is worth finding out what.

[Alice] Thirty days is your ordering rhythm.
[Alice] Now tap 30d.
[Alice] This is the one most people live in, because it lines up with how often orders actually get placed.
[Alice] A single quiet weekend or one heavy Monday stops mattering at this length, so the average you see here is close to what you should be buying.

[Alice] Ninety days shows the season.
[Alice] Tap 90d.
[Alice] Three months is long enough to see the shape of a year forming.
[Alice] Salt and windshield fluid climb into winter, filters and coolant climb into summer, and none of that is visible in a week.
[Alice] This is the range to check before you commit to a big order.

[Alice] All time is the honest average.
[Alice] Last one.
[Alice] All uses every movement ever recorded for this item, back to the first one.
[Alice] It is the fairest number you have for setting a reorder point, because it is not flattered by a good month or dragged down by a slow one.
[Alice] Whichever range you leave selected only changes what you are looking at, never the underlying history.

[Alice] Let the app pick the number for you.
[Alice] This card takes the average you were just looking at, adds about a week of cover, and suggests a reorder point from it.
[Alice] A week is an assumption, not a fact, because the app has no idea how long your supplier actually takes, so treat it as a sensible starting point rather than gospel.
[Alice] When there is a number here and an Apply button beside it, one tap sets it on the item.
[Alice] If it says there is not enough history yet, that is fine and expected on a fresh account: it fills itself in on its own once a few days of real use have been logged.

[Alice] Here is the fork in the road.
[Alice] Everything from here on is about the spreadsheet, so this is worth stopping on.
[Alice] Signing in with Google puts your inventory in a spreadsheet you own, readable from any computer, and still there if this phone goes in a puddle.
[Alice] If you want that, sign in now and I will walk you through sending it up and pulling it back.
[Alice] If you would rather not have a Google account tied to this, that is a completely fair answer, and you can close the tour with the X in the corner.
[Alice] Nothing you have learned so far depends on it.

[Alice] Push sends this device's copy up.
[Alice] Tap Push to Sheet now.
[Alice] It sends this device's current inventory up to your spreadsheet, and it is the half of syncing that people forget.
[Alice] Nothing goes up on its own.
[Alice] It happens when you tap this, and only when you tap this.

[Alice] Clear this device's copy.
[Alice] Tap Start Fresh whenever you are ready.
[Alice] Read this part carefully, because it is the one people get wrong.
[Alice] Start Fresh clears this device and only this device.
[Alice] It does not delete your Google Sheet, it does not empty it, and it does not change a single row in it.
[Alice] Your spreadsheet sits there exactly as you left it, which is why the very next step can bring the whole lot back down.

[Alice] Clear this device's copy.
[Alice] Start Fresh clears this device: the sample items, and anything you have added or changed while we have been talking.
[Alice] Since you have not connected a spreadsheet, there is nowhere to bring it back from afterwards, so this one is a one way trip today.
[Alice] That changes the moment you connect a sheet and push to it.
[Alice] Tap it if you want a clean slate to start your real stock on, or leave it alone and tap the arrow.

[Alice] Put a name on your changes.
[Alice] Add your name here so teammates working the same inventory can see who made a change and when.
[Alice] It's just a label, not a login, and anyone on this device can update it.

[Alice] Pull brings it back down.
[Alice] Now tap Pull from Sheet, and watch everything you just cleared come straight back.
[Alice] That is the whole point of the last three steps in one motion.
[Alice] Your inventory does not live on this phone.
[Alice] It lives in a spreadsheet you own, and this device is just one way of looking at it.

[Alice] Track equipment, not just stock.
[Alice] Property is a separate space for tracking equipment and fixtures, including ordered parts and maintenance status.
[Alice] It syncs to its own tab on the same spreadsheet.

[Alice] Reminders, and a home-screen shortcut.
[Alice] Turn on daily reminders and you'll only hear from us when something's actually worth checking.
[Alice] And if you'd like this app to feel less like a browser tab, you can install it right to your home screen from here.

[Alice] Come back to this tour any time.
[Alice] This link brings this exact walkthrough back whenever you want a refresher.
[Alice] It's the only way to see it again now, since it no longer opens automatically.

[Alice] That's the tour!
[Alice] You're all set.
[Alice] Explore Inventory on your own from here, or tap Manage Property above to keep going with equipment tracking.

property.text:
[Alice] It syncs to its own tab.
[Alice] Property gets its own tab on the same Google Sheet your inventory already uses.
[Alice] Push sends this device's list up to it, and Pull brings it back down.
[Alice] We will come back here at the end, once you have built something worth sending.

[Alice] Name the thing you look after.
[Alice] Tap Add property, and the form opens right where the button was.
[Alice] Give it a name you would actually recognize on a work order, like Washing Machine, Laundry Room.
[Alice] Location, serial number, and notes are all optional, so fill in what you know and leave the rest empty.
[Alice] Tap Add when you are happy with it, and I will pick things up from there.

[Alice] Let the part number do the typing.
[Alice] If you have a part number, off the old part or out of the manual, type it here and tap Look up.
[Alice] It fills in the description and a rough price for you, which beats typing all of it twice.
[Alice] When more than one product matches, it shows you the choices instead of guessing, and you pick the one that looks right.
[Alice] If you do not have a part number at all, skip this field completely.

[Alice] No part number? Describe it instead.
[Alice] This field is the only thing the form truly needs, and it is what you fall back on when there is no part number anywhere on the old part.
[Alice] Write it the way you would say it out loud to somebody behind a trade counter, like GE dryer drive belt.
[Alice] That description is also what gets searched when you go looking for it in a store in a moment, so a few extra words here save you scrolling through the wrong products later.

[Alice] Fill in what you know.
[Alice] Quantity, price, and an expected by date are all optional, but the expected date earns its five seconds.
[Alice] The row turns red on its own the day the part is late, so a delivery that quietly never arrived cannot hide from you.
[Alice] Tap Add part when you are done.

[Alice] Go and price it, I'll wait.
[Alice] Have not actually ordered it yet?
[Alice] Tap the cart icon and pick a store from the list that drops down.
[Alice] It searches that retailer for the description you just wrote, in a brand new tab, so you can compare prices, order it, and come straight back.
[Alice] This page will still be sitting right here waiting for you.
[Alice] Take as long as you need, and tap the arrow when you are back.

[Alice] Come back to this tour any time.
[Alice] This link brings this exact walkthrough back whenever you want a refresher.

[Alice] That's Property tracking!
[Alice] Everything you just built is real, and it is yours to keep.
[Alice] If you made the equipment up, the trash icon removes it and you can start again on the real thing.
[Alice] Close this with the X up in the corner whenever you are ready.
